title: Duty of candour & when things go wrong
blurb: Being open and honest when something goes wrong: the professional duty every registrant has, the statutory duty on CQC-registered providers, and your role as a dental nurse.
question: During a filling, you realise you gave the dentist the wrong shade of composite and it has already been placed and cured. The patient hasn't noticed. The dentist is about to dismiss her. What should happen now, and why?

teach.body: The duty of candour means being open and honest with patients when something goes wrong with their treatment or care that causes, or could cause, harm or distress. It is a professional duty for every GDC registrant, including dental nurses, set out in GDC guidance on being open and honest and in a joint statement by the UK healthcare regulators. Patients trust us to tell them the truth. Hiding a mistake turns an error into a breach of professional standards.

letters.sub: Promptly, when something has gone wrong
Offer to put matters right if possible
Be open with colleagues; report incidents and near misses

teach.caption: The same duty applies whether the patient is told directly or, where appropriate, someone acting on their behalf, such as a parent.

teach.h: An apology is not an admission of liability
teach.body: Many people fear that saying sorry means admitting negligence. It doesn't. In England and Wales the Compensation Act 2006 says an apology does not, of itself, amount to an admission of negligence, and indemnity providers encourage prompt, sincere apologies. Saying sorry is simply the right and human thing to do. What causes real damage, to the patient and to your registration, is covering up, delaying or asking colleagues to stay quiet.

rows.label: Triggered by
values: Any harm or distress, actual or potential

teach.caption: Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 applies to the organisation, in England. A notifiable safety incident is an unintended or unexpected incident that has caused, or could cause, significant harm such as death, serious injury, or prolonged pain or psychological harm; the exact definition depends on the type of provider. The devolved nations have their own statutory duties.

steps.label: Make safe
steps.sub: Deal with any immediate harm first

steps.label: Explain and remedy
steps.sub: What happened, effects, how it will be put right

teach.h: Your role as a dental nurse
teach.body: Usually the dentist leading the patient's care explains what happened to the patient, but candour is your duty too. If you make or spot a mistake, tell the dentist or a senior colleague immediately and give an honest account. Support the conversation with the patient, record what happened, and complete the incident report. Report near misses too, because they show where the next real incident could happen. Never alter records afterwards, and never agree to keep something quiet.

teach.text: Candour isn't just for the dentist, and it isn't optional if the patient 'didn't notice'. If something has gone wrong that could harm or distress them, they must be told. Waiting for the patient to ask is not being open.

items: Candour: be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong.
Professional duty (every registrant): tell, apologise, offer a remedy, explain the effects, take part in reviews.
Statutory duty (Regulation 20): CQC-registered providers, for notifiable safety incidents, in person then in writing.
An apology is not, of itself, an admission of negligence.
Report near misses, record honestly and never cover up.

summary: You can now explain the professional duty of candour every registrant has, the statutory duty on CQC-registered providers, what to say and do when something goes wrong, why an apology isn't an admission of liability, and why near misses must be reported too.

A.q: A dental nurse makes a mistake that could affect a patient's care. What does the duty of candour require?
options: Wait to see whether harm develops
Tell the patient what happened and apologise
Record it only in the incident log
Ask the dentist to decide whether to mention it
A.why: Candour means being open with the patient: telling them what has gone wrong and offering a sincere apology.

whyNot.0: Waiting deprives the patient of information they need now and is not being open.
whyNot.2: Recording is required, but the patient must also be told.
whyNot.3: The decision isn't whether to tell; the patient has a right to know.

A.q: To whom does the statutory duty of candour under Regulation 20 apply?
options: Every GDC registrant personally
Only dentists, not dental care professionals
CQC-registered providers of care
Only NHS hospital trusts
A.why: Regulation 20 places the statutory duty on organisations registered with the CQC, including dental practices in England.

whyNot.0: Individual registrants have the professional duty; the statutory duty is on the provider.
whyNot.1: All registrants have the professional duty; the statutory duty is on the organisation.
whyNot.3: It applies to all CQC-registered providers, not only hospital trusts.

A.q: A colleague worries that apologising to a patient will admit the practice was negligent. What is correct?
options: An apology always admits legal liability
Only written apologies can admit legal fault
An apology must wait for legal advice
An apology is not, of itself, an admission
A.why: In England and Wales the Compensation Act 2006 makes clear that an apology does not, of itself, admit negligence.

whyNot.0: This is a common myth; an apology alone is not an admission of liability.
whyNot.1: Neither spoken nor written apologies are, in themselves, admissions of liability.
whyNot.2: Delaying an apology for legal advice works against being open and honest.

B.q: Which is NOT part of the professional duty of candour?
options: Offering an apology
Explaining the likely effects
Offering a remedy or support
Waiting until the patient asks
B.why: Candour is proactive: you tell the patient when something has gone wrong, without waiting to be asked.

whyNot.0: Apologising is a core part of the duty.
whyNot.1: Explaining the short- and long-term effects is part of the duty.
whyNot.2: Offering to put matters right, where possible, is part of the duty.

B.q: You notice the wrong patient's radiograph is on screen and stop it before treatment starts. What should you do?
options: Report it as a near miss
Ignore it, as no harm was done
Tell the patient they nearly had the wrong treatment
Quietly fix the error and say nothing
B.why: Near misses should be reported so the practice can learn and prevent a real incident next time.

whyNot.1: No harm this time doesn't mean the risk has gone away; reporting helps prevent it.
whyNot.2: The patient was not affected, so the priority is internal reporting and learning.
whyNot.3: Saying nothing hides a system problem that could cause harm later.

B.q: Under the statutory duty, how must a notifiable safety incident first be communicated to the patient?
options: By text message only
In person, then in writing
In writing within one year
Only if the patient complains
B.why: The provider must tell the person in person as soon as reasonably practicable, then follow up with written notification.

whyNot.0: A text alone does not meet the requirement for an in-person account and apology.
whyNot.2: It must be as soon as reasonably practicable, not a year later.
whyNot.3: The duty applies whether or not the patient complains.

C.q: A dentist asks you not to mention to the patient that an instrument tip fractured during treatment. What should you do?
options: Agree, since the dentist leads the patient's care
Go and tell the patient yourself straight away
Say the patient must be told; escalate if not
Note it privately in case there is a complaint
C.why: You must not take part in a cover-up. Remind the dentist of the duty of candour and escalate if the patient is not told.

whyNot.0: Following an instruction to hide an incident breaches your own professional duty.
whyNot.1: Discuss it with the dentist first; the leading clinician normally explains and you escalate if they refuse.
whyNot.3: Private notes don't make the patient aware and suggest you knew but stayed silent.

C.q: Which of these best describes the duty of candour?
options: Being open and honest when things go wrong
Reporting colleagues to the GDC for mistakes
Keeping patients' information confidential
Gaining consent before every treatment
C.why: The duty of candour is about openness and honesty with patients when something goes wrong with their care.

whyNot.1: Candour is about the patient being told; referrals to the GDC are only for serious concerns.
whyNot.2: Confidentiality is a separate duty about protecting patient information.
whyNot.3: Consent is a separate duty that comes before treatment, not after an incident.

C.q: After an incident has been explained to the patient, what should happen next?
options: Delete the related appointment notes
Record it and review it to learn
Move the patient to another dentist
Offer a refund in exchange for silence
C.why: Recording the incident and reviewing it helps the team understand what went wrong and stop it happening again.

whyNot.0: Records must never be deleted or altered to hide an incident.
whyNot.2: Changing dentist may be the patient's choice, but it doesn't replace learning from the incident.
whyNot.3: Asking for silence in exchange for money is dishonest and unprofessional.

reteach.title: Honesty is the safety net
reteach.question: Think of a time someone owned up to a mistake straight away. How did that compare with finding out later that something had been hidden from you?

blocks.body: When a mechanic says 'I'm sorry, I fitted the wrong part. Here's what it means and we'll replace it free', you might be annoyed, but you trust them. If you found out months later they'd hidden it, you'd never go back. Patients feel the same. Being open quickly (tell, apologise, explain, put it right) keeps trust, and reporting the incident helps the whole team learn. Hiding it harms the patient and puts your registration at risk.

explain.body: Every registrant must tell the patient when something has gone wrong, apologise, offer a remedy or support, and fully explain the short- and long-term effects. They must also be open with colleagues and take part in reviews.

test.q: Which set of actions best matches the professional duty of candour?
options: Record, refer, discharge
Tell, apologise, explain, put right
Investigate, then decide what to say
Refund, apologise, close the file
test.why: The duty is to tell the patient, apologise, explain the effects and offer to put matters right.

whyNot.0: Discharging a patient isn't part of candour.
whyNot.2: Telling the patient shouldn't wait for an investigation to decide what to reveal.
whyNot.3: A refund may be part of a remedy but closing the file misses explanation and learning.

explain.body: Regulation 20 applies to CQC-registered providers in England. For a notifiable safety incident, the provider must tell the person in person as soon as reasonably practicable, give an account and apology, then follow up in writing and keep records.

items.label: Told in person, with an apology

test.q: Who holds the statutory duty of candour in a CQC-registered dental practice?
options: The patient's GP
The GDC
The registered provider
The dental nurse on duty alone
test.why: The statutory duty sits with the registered provider (the organisation), alongside each registrant's professional duty.

whyNot.0: The GP is not responsible for incidents in the dental practice.
whyNot.1: The GDC regulates individuals; the statutory duty is enforced through CQC registration.
whyNot.3: The nurse has a professional duty, but the statutory duty is on the provider.

explain.body: An apology is not, of itself, an admission of negligence. Near misses, where an error is caught before reaching the patient, should still be reported so the team can learn.

test.q: Why should near misses be reported if no one was harmed?
options: To identify a risk before it causes harm
So the patient can claim compensation
Because the GDC must be told of every one
To show which staff member was at fault
test.why: Near-miss reports reveal weaknesses in systems so they can be fixed before a patient is actually harmed.

whyNot.1: No harm occurred, so compensation is not the purpose.
whyNot.2: Near misses are reported within the practice, not routinely to the GDC.
whyNot.3: Reporting is about learning and safety, not blame.
